Issued at 430 AM CDT Thu Aug 27 2026

Areas of fog are still possible this morning across anywhere
with clear skies and light winds. Meanwhile, wildfire smoke
trapped under the inversion could also reduce visibility this 
morning. Otherwise ridging aloft will prevail while the surface 
high moves eastward through the day. Some convergence this 
morning has allowed for a few thunderstorms in central MT to 
develop. A few CAMs have this activity following a gradient of 
weak instability and moving into southwestern ND later today. 
Dry air in place and ridging aloft should limit these chances, 
these kept a mainly dry forecast for today. As the surface high 
moves eastward winds will switch to the east southeast from a 
developing surface low to the west. This steady wind combined 
with low RH values may bring a brief period of elevated fire 
weather concerns to the far west today, although the overall 
fire weather concerns should remain low. Southerly flow will 
also slightly warm temperatures into the upper 70s to upper 80s 
today, with some lower 90s in the west. Wildfire smoke aloft 
could linger today, although smoke at the surface remains 
uncertain given the lack of flow becoming a southerly flow. 
Tonight, an elevated warm front and encroaching surface low 
will return chances for showers and thunderstorms to the west 
and some central areas. Although surface based instability is 
low, elevated instability could be modest later tonight and 
Friday morning. This combined with some modest shear could 
produce and isolated strong to severe storm, especially if a low
level jet can set up across the west. Multi-cluster nature of 
these storms would limit the severe threat, although perhaps 
some near severe criteria hail and winds are possible. SPC for 
now has general risk for thunder in these areas through tonight,
as capping and timing of the waves remain uncertain. Thus will 
continue to monitor for any trends for higher confidence in 
strong to severe thunderstorms tonight into Friday morning. 
Lows tonight will generally be in the 50s to lower 60s. Friday, 
surface low further develops across the northern high plains, 
while a warm front lifts across much of the state. Most areas 
will see above normal temperatures in the 80s to lower 90s as a 
result. Some breezy southerly winds will also be found with this
front. Fire weather concerns look to remain low as the drier air 
in the west looks to be removed from the more breezier winds in 
the central and east. The main concern for Friday still remains 
the chance for isolated severe thunderstorms. SPC has maintained
a Marginal Risk for severe weather in south central and 
southeastern portions. Still fairly conditional on storms 
breaking through the cap and developing along this warm front. 
This is if the morning convection doesn't impact storms 
developing later in the day as well. If this cap can be broken,
there is a window of strong shear and ample instability for 
severe storms. Main hazards would likely be hail up to golf 
balls and 70 mph with any discrete cells that could form, and 
slightly lower hail and wind if storm mode remains multicluster.
The tornado threat remains low, although there are times STP is
around 1. LCLs may be a bit high for the tornado threat, and 
the uncertainty with storm mode is also of concern. Showers and 
thunderstorms could then linger through the night Friday night, 
with low in the 50s. 

An unsettled pattern looks to remain for Saturday as the surface
low stalls across the region and a potent shortwave moves
through. Given modest instability and shear, isolated severe
thunderstorms will be possible to much of the CWA. SPC has a
Marginal Risk for much of the CWA on Saturday as a result. Of
note for Saturday is the potential for some heavy rain as the
mentioned shortwave brings with it a plume of Pacific moisture.
As a result Pwats look to be elevated for Saturday, and WPC
currently has a Marginal Risk for excessive rainfall. The
heaviest rain may be thunderstorm dependent yet worth
monitoring. With this southwest flow aloft temperatures will
remain warm and generally in the 80s on Saturday. A weak cold
front combined with a broad upper low then looks to move through
Sunday, slightly cooling temperatures and continuing chances 
for showers and thunderstorms. Instability looks more limited 
Sunday, although shear remains high. Thus an isolated strong to 
severe storm is possible. Another plume of Pacific moisture 
could again bring some heavy rain to the area on Sunday, with 
WPC placing a Marginal Risk in the north. Southwest to zonal 
flow aloft could keep periodic disturbances moving through the 
area through early to mid next week. Thus at least slight 
chances for showers and thunderstorms remain in the forecast 
each day. Some breezy westerly winds could be found to start 
next week behind Sunday's system. This combined with drier are 
could bring some increased fire weather concerns early next 
week. O
